title: Torpedo Grass in Rice Fields: How to Spot and Dig It Out
metaTitle: Torpedo Grass in Rice: How to Spot It and Stop It
metaDescription: Torpedo grass spreads from tough rootstocks on your bunds into rainfed palay. Learn how to spot it and how to dig it out before it takes over.
excerpt: Torpedo grass is a creeping perennial grass weed of rainfed lowland rice fields and the bunds of irrigated fields in the Philippines. It spreads through tough underground rootstocks with sharp, pointed tips. This page shows how to spot it, how it hurts your palay and how to control it.

heroImage.alt: Torpedo grass (Panicum repens), a grass weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Forest and Kim Starr, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Torpedo grass (Panicum repens) belongs to the grass family. Farmers know it by many local names, such as tagik tagik, buwag buwag, murag bermuda, maralaya, luy a luy a, sabilau and luya luyahan. A name like murag bermuda shows how often people mix it up with Bermuda grass. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields and along the bunds of irrigated fields.

This weed is a perennial, so it lives on from season to season. It makes seeds, but it spreads mainly through its rootstocks. These are tough stems that run under the soil and end in sharp, pointed tips. Every broken piece can grow into a new plant. So plowing a patch can spread it across the whole paddy.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about torpedo grass
rows: Tagik tagik, buwag buwag, murag bermuda, maralaya, luy a luy a, sabilau, luya luyahan
Rainfed lowland rice fields and along bunds of irrigated fields

blocks.text: Like other grasses, it has round, hollow stems with clear joints, or nodes. The stems stand upright and root at the nodes, which are smooth and hairless. The leaves are long, narrow, flat and slightly hairy. Its seed head is an open panicle with slender, upright branches. Small oval spikelets hang from thin stalks. Then dig around the base, and you will find the hard rootstocks with their sharp, pointed tips.

items: Upright stems rise from creeping rootstocks and root at the smooth, hairless nodes.
Leaves are long, narrow and flat, with a light coat of hairs.
The open panicle has slender, upright branches with small oval spikelets on thin stalks.
Underground stems end in hard, sharp tips that look like little torpedoes.
Look alike tip: Bermuda grass has two or three leaves at each runner joint, while this grass does not.
Patches often start on the bunds and creep into the paddy from the edges.

blocks.text:
As a perennial, this grass already has roots in the soil when you plant your rice. Its rootstocks hold stored food, so new shoots come up fast. Then they race your young palay for water, light and fertilizer. Thick patches crowd the rice hills along the field edges first, then move inward.

It also makes weeding slow and costly. Pulling the tops does not kill it, because the rootstocks stay alive in the soil. Each piece left behind sends up new shoots. On the bunds, it gives pests a place to hide between crops. Its seeds can also mix with your harvest when the patch reaches the rice.

items: Dig out each clump with all of its rootstocks. Follow the runners under the soil, since every piece left behind can regrow.
Keep the bunds of irrigated fields clean, because this grass often grows there first and then creeps into the paddy.
Rake rootstock pieces out after plowing and dry them in the sun on high ground, away from the field.
Check cleared spots again after a few weeks, and dig out any new shoots while they are still small.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Grasses

If water and weeding cannot hold torpedo grass down, choose an active ingredient that works on grasses at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Torpedo Grass Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before the seed heads open, and clean the thresher and harvester before they enter the field.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [grass weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Torpedo Grass

items.q: What do farmers call torpedo grass in the Philippines?
items.a: Farmers know it as tagik tagik, buwag buwag, murag bermuda, maralaya, luy a luy a, sabilau or luya luyahan. Its scientific name is Panicum repens. The name murag bermuda shows that people often confuse it with Bermuda grass. Here is a quick check: Bermuda grass has two or three leaves at each runner joint, and this weed does not.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention matters most. Keep bunds clean, dig out patches with their rootstocks before land preparation and rake out broken pieces after plowing. Water alone will not drown it, so hand weed and dig out new shoots early. If you need a herbicide, choose one for grass weeds that fits the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does torpedo grass come back after plowing?
items.a: Because plowing cuts its rootstocks into pieces, and each piece can grow into a new plant. The rootstocks store food, so the pieces sprout fast. Instead of plowing a patch right away, dig it out first. Then rake up the leftover pieces and dry them in the sun before you prepare the field.
